claim: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) are lined with intrinsically disordered FG-domains.
source: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) lined with intrinsically disordered FG-domains act as selective gatekeepers for molecular transport between the nucleus and the cytoplasm in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the structural composition of NPCs, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: NPCs act as selective gatekeepers for molecular transport between the nucleus and the cytoplasm in eukaryotic cells.
source: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) lined with intrinsically disordered FG-domains act as selective gatekeepers for molecular transport between the nucleus and the cytoplasm in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a well-established function of NPCs in cell biology.

claim: The physical mechanism underlying NPC selectivity is still under debate.
source: The underlying physical mechanism of the intriguing selectivity is still under debate.
evidence: This statement acknowledges the current state of scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Biomimetic NPCs consisting of Nsp1 domains attached to solid-state nanopores were used to probe transport of ions and transport receptors.
source: Here, we probe the transport of ions and transport receptors through biomimetic NPCs consisting of Nsp1 domains attached to the inner surface of solid-state nanopores.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Both wildtype FG-domains and hydrophilic SG-mutants were examined.
source: We examine both wildtype FG-domains and hydrophilic SG-mutants.
evidence: This describes the experimental design comparing two variants.

claim: FG-nanopores showed clear selectivity as transport receptors can translocate across the pore whereas other proteins cannot.
source: FG-nanopores showed a clear selectivity as transport receptors can translocate across the pore whereas other proteins cannot.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding from the study.

claim: SG mutant pores lack selectivity.
source: SG mutant pores lack such selectivity.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding comparing the mutant to wildtype.

claim: FG-pores exhibit a high-density, nonuniform protein distribution.
source: To unravel this striking difference, we present coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations that reveal that FG-pores exhibit a high-density, nonuniform protein distribution, in contrast to a uniform and significantly less-dense protein distribution in the SG-mutant.
evidence: This is a finding from the molecular dynamics simulations presented in the study.

claim: SG-mutant pores exhibit a uniform and significantly less-dense protein distribution compared to FG-pores.
source: To unravel this striking difference, we present coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations that reveal that FG-pores exhibit a high-density, nonuniform protein distribution, in contrast to a uniform and significantly less-dense protein distribution in the SG-mutant.
evidence: This is a finding from the molecular dynamics simulations presented in the study.

claim: The sequence-dependent density distribution of disordered proteins inside the NPC plays a key role for its conductivity and selective permeability.
source: We conclude that the sequence-dependent density distribution of disordered proteins inside the NPC plays a key role for its conductivity and selective permeability.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and computational results.

claim: NPCs have a molecular mass of around 100 MDa.
source: NPCs are giant structures with a molecular mass of around 100 MDa, composed of about 30 different types of proteins named nucleoporins (Nups) (Hurt and Beck, 2015; Hoelz et al., 2016; Schwartz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NPCs are composed of about 30 different types of proteins named nucleoporins (Nups).
source: NPCs are giant structures with a molecular mass of around 100 MDa, composed of about 30 different types of proteins named nucleoporins (Nups) (Hurt and Beck, 2015; Hoelz et al., 2016; Schwartz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NPCs are permeable for molecules of up to 30 kDa or ~5 nm in diameter.
source: NPCs are equipped with a barrier that is permeable for molecules of up to 30 kDa or ~5 nm in diameter, but blocks the passage of larger ones (Popken et al., 2015; Schmidt and Görlich, 2016; Timney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NPCs block the passage of molecules larger than 30 kDa or ~5 nm in diameter.
source: NPCs are equipped with a barrier that is permeable for molecules of up to 30 kDa or ~5 nm in diameter, but blocks the passage of larger ones (Popken et al., 2015; Schmidt and Görlich, 2016; Timney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Shuttling nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) can overcome the size-limit and traverse the NPC.
source: Shuttling nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) can overcome this size-limit and traverse the NPC, carrying along cargoes with diameters of up to 40 nm (Panté and Kann, 2002; Lowe et al., 2010), thus endowing the pore with a selective permeability barrier.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NTRs can carry cargoes with diameters of up to 40 nm through the NPC.
source: Shuttling nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) can overcome this size-limit and traverse the NPC, carrying along cargoes with diameters of up to 40 nm (Panté and Kann, 2002; Lowe et al., 2010), thus endowing the pore with a selective permeability barrier.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nups that contain phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats (FG-Nups) are crucial for NPC selectivity.
source: Nups that contain phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats (FG-Nups) (Hurt, 1988) are crucial for this remarkable selectivity, suggesting that the NTR transport is mediated by hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: NTR transport is mediated by hydrophobic interactions.
source: Nups that contain phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats (FG-Nups) (Hurt, 1988) are crucial for this remarkable selectivity, suggesting that the NTR transport is mediated by hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the importance of FG repeats.

claim: FG-repeat domains are intrinsically disordered.
source: The FG-repeat domains are intrinsically disordered, bind NTRs during facilitated translocation (Iovine et al., 1995; Bayliss et al., 1999), and form the NPC permeability barrier (Frey and Görlich, 2007; Patel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FG-repeat domains bind NTRs during facilitated translocation.
source: The FG-repeat domains are intrinsically disordered, bind NTRs during facilitated translocation (Iovine et al., 1995; Bayliss et al., 1999), and form the NPC permeability barrier (Frey and Görlich, 2007; Patel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FG-repeat domains form the NPC permeability barrier.
source: The FG-repeat domains are intrinsically disordered, bind NTRs during facilitated translocation (Iovine et al., 1995; Bayliss et al., 1999), and form the NPC permeability barrier (Frey and Görlich, 2007; Patel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A typical NPC comprises about 10–12 different FG Nups in copy numbers of 8 to 32.
source: A typical NPC comprises about 10–12 different FG Nups (in copy numbers of 8 to 32), yielding about 5000 FG motifs per NPC.
evidence: This is a statement about NPC composition based on established knowledge.

claim: A typical NPC contains about 5000 FG motifs.
source: A typical NPC comprises about 10–12 different FG Nups (in copy numbers of 8 to 32), yielding about 5000 FG motifs per NPC.
evidence: This is calculated from the number and copy numbers of FG Nups.

claim: S. cerevisiae Nsp1 is one of the most abundant and best-studied FG Nups.
source: One of the most abundant and best-studied FG Nups is S. cerevisiae Nsp1 (Hurt, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the Nsp1-SG variant, hydrophobic amino acids F, I, L and V are replaced by hydrophilic serines (S).
source: Here, we specifically address the importance of FG domains for NPCs by comparing the transport properties of Nsp1-coated biomimetic NPCs with analogs that employ an Nsp1 mutant in which the hydrophobic amino acids F, I, L and V are replaced by hydrophilic serines (S), thus creating an 'SG' Nsp1 variant.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the mutant protein.

claim: The mutated Nsp1-SG domain was unable to form a hydrogel-like structure.
source: In earlier studies, it was shown that the mutated Nsp1-SG domain was unable to form a hydrogel-like structure (Frey et al., 2006; Patel et al., 2007; Ader et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: For Nsp1-coated pores, the conductance dropped about 80% after coating.
source: For the Nsp1-coated pores, the conductance G =I/V dropped about 80% after coating Nsp1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For pores coated with Nsp1-S, the current drop was about 50% when compared with bare pores.
source: For pores coated with Nsp1-S, the current drop was lower, about 50% when compared with bare pores (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The difference in current blockade between Nsp1 and Nsp1-S points towards a different volumetric arrangement of the proteins inside the nanopore.
source: The difference in the current blockade points towards a different volumetric arrangement of the proteins inside the nanopore, thus emphasizing the difference in the amino acid sequence of Nsp1 and Nsp1-S.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental conductance data.

claim: For bare pores, a conductance of G = 6–88 nS was measured for pore diameters ranging from 5 to 60 nm.
source: For bare pores, a conductance of G = 6–88 nS was measured for pore diameters ranging from 5 to 60 nm.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement.

claim: Nsp1-coated pores show two distinct regimes of ion conductivity above and below a threshold diameter of 41 ± 2 nm.
source: For Nsp1-coated pores, the conductance data show a radically different behaviour, with two rather distinct regimes of ion conductivity above and below an apparent threshold diameter of dNsp1 = 41 ± 2 nm.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from conductance measurements.

claim: Nsp1-coated pores with diameter ranging from 5 nm to 41 nm showed a very low conductance of G = 0.2 to 4 nS.
source: The current measured for pores with a diameter ranging from 5 nm to 41 nm showed a very low conductance of G = 0.2 to 4 nS (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement referenced in a supplementary figure.

claim: Nsp1-S-coated pores have a threshold diameter of 23 ± 3 nm.
source: When we coat the pores with the Nsp1-S mutant, we observed a qualitatively similar non-linear G(d) behaviour as for the Nsp1-coated pores, but with a much lower threshold diameter dNsp1-S = 23 ± 3 nm.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from conductance measurements.

claim: The MD model is based on a one-bead-per-amino-acid representation that distinguishes between all 20 amino acids.
source: The MD model of the domains is based on a one-bead-per-amino-acid representation that distinguishes between all 20 amino acids (see Figure 2A) (Ghavami et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the computational model used, with citation to previous work.

claim: The model takes into account hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions between amino acids, as well as the screening effect of free ions and the polarity of the solvent.
source: The model takes into account hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions between the amino acids, as well as the screening effect of free ions and the polarity of the solvent.
evidence: This describes features of the computational model.

claim: The model has been shown to accurately predict (within 20% error) the Stokes radii of a wide range of FG domains and FG domain segments.
source: The model has been shown to accurately predict (within 20% error) the Stokes radii of a wide range of FG domains and FG domain segments (Ghavami et al., 2014), including the low-charge Nsp11-172 and high-charge Nsp1173-603 FG segments (Yamada et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a validation of the model based on previous work.

claim: Nsp1 and Nsp1-S were anchored in a close-packed triangular lattice with an average grafting density of 1 per 28 nm2.
source: The Nsp1 and Nsp1-S were anchored in a close-packed triangular lattice with an average grafting density of 1 per 28 nm2, corresponding to an average grafting distance of 5.7 nm.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the computational model.

claim: The grafting distance of 5.7 nm was experimentally estimated using two independent techniques.
source: This grafting distance was experimentally estimated using two independent techniques (see Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Figure 1—figure supplement 5; Figure 1—figure supplement 6), and further confirmed in experiments on denatured proteins in guanidinium HCl (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes experimental validation of a model parameter.

claim: The 1 per 28 nm2 grafting density matches well with the surface area per FG Nup in a yeast NPC of about 24 to 32 nm2.
source: The 1 per 28 nm2 grafting density matches well with the surface area per FG Nup in a yeast NPC of about 24 to 32 nm2 and is close to the density that was reported for Nsp1 assembled in vitro on a planar surface (Eisele et al., 2013).
evidence: This compares the model parameter to known biological values, supported by citation.

claim: The mass density inside the central cylindrical region of the larger Nsp1 pores is much higher (70–100 mg/ml) than that for the mutant (50 mg/ml).
source: The mass density inside the central cylindrical region of the larger Nsp1 pores is much higher (70–100 mg/ml), than that for the mutant (50 mg/ml), as can also be seen in the z-averaged (−10 nm <z < 10 nm) radial density distribution in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is a result from the MD simulations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Nsp1 pores feature a maximum density at the central axis.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the Nsp1 pores clearly feature a maximum density at the central axis (r = 0, see Figure 3), which is possibly related to the high percentage of hydrophobic residues, relative to charged residues, in the head group of the wildtype Nsp1.
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The maximum density at the central axis in Nsp1 pores is possibly related to the high percentage of hydrophobic residues in the head group of wildtype Nsp1.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the Nsp1 pores clearly feature a maximum density at the central axis (r = 0, see Figure 3), which is possibly related to the high percentage of hydrophobic residues, relative to charged residues, in the head group of the wildtype Nsp1.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed density distribution.

claim: Nsp1-S data show a much more uniform and less dense distribution compared to wildtype Nsp1.
source: The Nsp1-S data show a striking difference in density distribution: much more uniform and less dense, which is likely to be caused by the lower number of hydrophobic residues compared to the wildtype Nsp1 (see Figure 2C and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations shown in Figures 2C and 3A.

claim: The uniform and less dense distribution in Nsp1-S is likely caused by the lower number of hydrophobic residues compared to wildtype Nsp1.
source: The Nsp1-S data show a striking difference in density distribution: much more uniform and less dense, which is likely to be caused by the lower number of hydrophobic residues compared to the wildtype Nsp1 (see Figure 2C and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed density distribution.

claim: For Nsp1, the heads are rather localized, forming a cohesive structure around the central pore axis for the 45 and 60 nm pores.
source: Our results show that for Nsp1 the heads are rather localized, forming a cohesive structure around the central pore axis for the 45 (see Video 1) and 60 nm pores.
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations shown in Video 1.

claim: Nsp1-S heads show a much more widespread distribution compared to Nsp1.
source: In contrast, the Nsp1-S heads show a much more widespread distribution (see Video 2), reflecting their higher charge-to-hydrophobicity ratio.
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations shown in Video 2.

claim: The Stokes radii of the head and stalk region of Nsp1 are 3.2 nm and 6.5 nm, respectively.
source: The Stokes radii (RS) of the head and stalk region are 3.2 nm and 6.5 nm, respectively, as computed by us (Ghavami et al., 2014) and measured by Yamada and coworkers (Yamada et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by computational results and citations to previous measurements.

claim: For the smaller pore size of 22 nm, the geometric confinement pushes the Nsp1 heads out from the core of the pore.
source: It is interesting to note that the radii of gyration of the head and stalk region in isolation are similar as when they are part of one Nsp1 molecule. However, the radius of gyration of Nsp1 is less than the sum of the radius of gyration of the head and tail, indicating that the head and tail do interact but retain their individual conformation (see Video 3), even when tethered together (see SI Video 1). This also carries over to their conformation inside the pore, albeit with one difference: the radius of gyration of the stalk region is enlarged by 30%, whereas the radius of gyration of the head again remains unchanged. This is most likely caused by the stronger lateral constraints of the stalks at the anchor points (C-terminal), while the N-terminal heads have more freedom.
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations.

claim: The radius of gyration of Nsp1 is less than the sum of the radius of gyration of the head and tail, indicating that the head and tail do interact but retain their individual conformation.
source: It is interesting to note that the radii of gyration of the head and stalk region in isolation are similar as when they are part of one Nsp1 molecule. However, the radius of gyration of Nsp1 is less than the sum of the radius of gyration of the head and tail, indicating that the head and tail do interact but retain their individual conformation (see Video 3), even when tethered together (see SI Video 1).
evidence: This is an inference from computational measurements shown in Video 3.

claim: The radius of gyration of the stalk region is enlarged by 30% inside the pore, whereas the radius of gyration of the head remains unchanged.
source: This also carries over to their conformation inside the pore, albeit with one difference: the radius of gyration of the stalk region is enlarged by 30%, whereas the radius of gyration of the head again remains unchanged.
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations.

claim: The enlargement of the stalk region radius of gyration is most likely caused by the stronger lateral constraints of the stalks at the anchor points, while the N-terminal heads have more freedom.
source: This is most likely caused by the stronger lateral constraints of the stalks at the anchor points (C-terminal), while the N-terminal heads have more freedom.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed structural changes.

claim: Nup98 FG domain has a low charge-to-hydrophobicity ratio, resulting in a collapsed structure.
source: The Nup98 FG domain has a low charge-to-hydrophobicity ratio, resulting in a collapsed structure, and it is grafted on the pore surface at a density of 1 per 49 nm2 (Kowalczyk et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Nup98 is grafted on the pore surface at a density of 1 per 49 nm2.
source: The Nup98 FG domain has a low charge-to-hydrophobicity ratio, resulting in a collapsed structure, and it is grafted on the pore surface at a density of 1 per 49 nm2 (Kowalczyk et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Nup98 FG pore shows a very dense (300 mg/ml) ring-like structure that forms already at relatively small pore sizes (25–30 nm).
source: The 2D (r,z) and radial density distribution, depicted in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, show a profoundly different behaviour: the Nup98 FG pore shows a very dense (300 mg/ml) ring-like structure that forms already at relatively small pore sizes (25–30 nm), while the protein density vanishes towards the pore centre.
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Nup98 pores, the protein density vanishes towards the pore centre.
source: The 2D (r,z) and radial density distribution, depicted in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, show a profoundly different behaviour: the Nup98 FG pore shows a very dense (300 mg/ml) ring-like structure that forms already at relatively small pore sizes (25–30 nm), while the protein density vanishes towards the pore centre.
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ionic conductance through Nup98 pores only commences when a central conduit has opened up in the nonconductive high-density ring structure.
source: The key observation is that, consistent with experiments (Kowalczyk et al., 2011b), the ionic conductance through the Nup98 pores only commences when a central conduit has opened up in the nonconductive high-density ring structure, which contrast Nsp1 and Nsp1-S pores that are filled by a uniform protein network of relative low density that supports ion flow throughout (see below).
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations, consistent with previous experiments.

claim: The experimental and theoretical conductance data are in good quantitative agreement.
source: Gratifyingly, the experimental and theoretical data are even in good quantitative agreement (see inset Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental and computational results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The conductance of a single NPC is quite low, with values of only 0.3–2 nS.
source: However, the conductance of a single NPC is actually quite low, with values of only 0.3–2 nS, which is roughly two orders of magnitude lower than unhindered ionic transport (Bustamante et al., 1995; Tonini et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous measurements.

claim: The biomimetic NPC with only Nsp1 has a conductance of ~4 nS for 35 nm pores, which is quite close to the in vivo value of 0.3–2 nS.
source: It is noteworthy that our biomimetic NPC, with only 1 type of Nups, viz. Nsp1, has a conductance of ~4 nS for 35 nm pores, which is quite close to the in vivo value of 0.3–2 nS, certainly in view of the simplicity of our biomimetic NPC.
evidence: This is a comparison between the experimental biomimetic system and natural NPCs.

claim: Kap95 translocates through Nsp1-coated pores with a most likely translocation time of τ = 5.2 ms±2.4 ms.
source: Kap95 translocate through such pores with a most likely translocation time of τ = 5.2 ms±2.4 ms and an average conductance blockade of 0.31 ± 0.10 nS (N = 3).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement from translocation experiments.

claim: Kap95 translocates through Nsp1-coated pores with an average conductance blockade of 0.31 ± 0.10 nS.
source: Kap95 translocate through such pores with a most likely translocation time of τ = 5.2 ms±2.4 ms and an average conductance blockade of 0.31 ± 0.10 nS (N = 3).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement from translocation experiments.

claim: The significant increase in translocation time of Kap95 through Nsp1-coated pores indicates interactions between Nsp1 and Kap95.
source: The most noteworthy difference is the significant increase in translocation time of Kap95 as it moves through the Nsp1-coated pore, indicating interactions between Nsp1 and Kap95.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental translocation time measurements.

claim: Passage of tCherry through Nsp1-coated pores was essentially blocked, with only n = 90 events compared to n = 917 for Kap95 in the same time window and at the same concentration.
source: We found that passage of tCherry through the Nsp1-coated pores was essentially blocked: The tCherry translocation experiments yielded a significantly lower number of events (n = 90, compared to n = 917 for Kap95 in the same time window and at the same concentration; see Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The Nsp1-coated pore is selective: it does not allow tCherry to pass through efficiently, in contrast to the transport observed for Kap95.
source: From these measurements, we conclude that the Nsp1-coated pore is selective: it does not allow tCherry to pass through efficiently, in contrast to the transport observed for Kap95.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental translocation data.

claim: Kap95 translocates through Nsp1-S-coated pores with an average translocation time of τ = 0.23 ± 0.13 ms.
source: We successfully performed such experiments (Figure 4D and F), yielding an average translocation time for Kap95 of τ = 0.23 ± 0.13 ms (Figure 4D) and τ = 0.45 ± 0.23 ms for tCherry (Figure 4F), and a conductance blockade of 0.24 ± 0.10 nS and 0.32 ± 0.09 nS, respectively (N = 3).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 4D.

claim: tCherry translocates through Nsp1-S-coated pores with an average translocation time of τ = 0.45 ± 0.23 ms.
source: We successfully performed such experiments (Figure 4D and F), yielding an average translocation time for Kap95 of τ = 0.23 ± 0.13 ms (Figure 4D) and τ = 0.45 ± 0.23 ms for tCherry (Figure 4F), and a conductance blockade of 0.24 ± 0.10 nS and 0.32 ± 0.09 nS, respectively (N = 3).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Kap95 and tCherry translocate mutant-coated pores very well with short translocation times, similar to those for bare pores.
source: We thus find that the Kap95 and tCherry actually translocate mutant-coated pores very well with short translocation times, similar to those for bare pores.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental translocation data.

claim: The selectivity of the Nsp1-coated pores is lost when the hydrophobic FG-domains are replaced by the hydrophilic SG-domains.
source: The data show that the selectivity of the Nsp1-coated pores is lost when the hydrophobic FG-domains are replaced by the hydrophilic SG-domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the translocation data of Nsp1 and Nsp1-S pores.

claim: The measured event rate of Kap95 was 1.7 ± 0.2 Hz for a bare pore, 1.4 ± 0.3 Hz for Nsp1-coated pores, and 1.4 ± 0.1 Hz for Nsp1-S-coated pores.
source: The measured event rate of Kap95 was 1.7 ± 0.2 Hz for a bare pore, 1.4 ± 0.3 Hz for Nsp1-coated pores, and 1.4 ± 0.1 Hz for Nsp1-S-coated pores, i.e., Kap95 thus translocates through all pore types with a similar event rate.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement of event frequencies.

claim: Kap95 translocates through all pore types with a similar event rate.
source: The measured event rate of Kap95 was 1.7 ± 0.2 Hz for a bare pore, 1.4 ± 0.3 Hz for Nsp1-coated pores, and 1.4 ± 0.1 Hz for Nsp1-S-coated pores, i.e., Kap95 thus translocates through all pore types with a similar event rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the event frequency measurements.

claim: A constant baseline current was observed at all Kap95 concentrations in Nsp1-coated pores.
source: Additionally, we performed translocation measurements for varying Kap95 concentration (50–500 nM) through a Nsp1-coated pore, where we observed a constant baseline current at all Kap95 concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), contrasting to what would have been the case if large numbers of Kap95 would accumulate within the pore (Lim et al., 2015; Kapinos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A linear increase in event frequency was observed with increasing Kap95 concentration.
source: Furthermore, we observed, as expected, a linear increase in the event frequency (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: tCherry virtually fails to pass through Nsp1-coated pores with an event frequency as low as 0.02 ± 0.04 Hz at 100 nM concentration.
source: Notably, in contrast to the finite 1.4 Hz event rate measured for Kap95, tCherry virtually fails to pass through the Nsp1-coated pores with an event frequency as low as 0.02 ± 0.04 Hz (at the same 100 nM concentration), while it translocates easily through the bare and Nsp1-S pores, with frequencies of 1.3 ± 0.2 Hz and 1.2 ± 0.3 Hz, respectively.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement of event frequencies.

claim: tCherry translocates easily through bare and Nsp1-S pores, with frequencies of 1.3 ± 0.2 Hz and 1.2 ± 0.3 Hz, respectively.
source: Notably, in contrast to the finite 1.4 Hz event rate measured for Kap95, tCherry virtually fails to pass through the Nsp1-coated pores with an event frequency as low as 0.02 ± 0.04 Hz (at the same 100 nM concentration), while it translocates easily through the bare and Nsp1-S pores, with frequencies of 1.3 ± 0.2 Hz and 1.2 ± 0.3 Hz, respectively.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement of event frequencies.

claim: No clear diameter dependence of the selectivity was noted for Nsp1-S-coated pores in the range of 32 nm to 50 nm.
source: Event frequencies for translocation through Nsp1-S-coated pores were also tested for various pore sizes in the range of 32 nm to 50 nm (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) for both Kap95 and tCherry. No clear diameter dependence of the selectivity was noted.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: tCherry is simulated as an inert sphere of radius 7.4 nm.
source: tCherry is simulated by using an inert (Cardarelli et al., 2011) sphere of radius 7.4 nm (see Supplementary file 1) while for Kap95 we use a sphere of radius 8.5 nm that is covered by 10 hydrophobic binding spots and a total charge of −43e (Kersey et al., 2012) homogeneously distributed on the surface (Tagliazucchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the computational model for tCherry, with citation.

claim: Kap95 is simulated as a sphere of radius 8.5 nm covered by 10 hydrophobic binding spots and a total charge of −43e.
source: tCherry is simulated by using an inert (Cardarelli et al., 2011) sphere of radius 7.4 nm (see Supplementary file 1) while for Kap95 we use a sphere of radius 8.5 nm that is covered by 10 hydrophobic binding spots and a total charge of −43e (Kersey et al., 2012) homogeneously distributed on the surface (Tagliazucchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the computational model for Kap95, with citations.

claim: The energy barrier that tCherry needs to overcome to move across the Nsp1-lined pore is approximately 12 kJ/mol.
source: The data show that the energy barrier that tCherry needs to overcome to move across the Nsp1-lined pore is approximately 12 kJ/mol, while for Kap95, it is much lower, 6 kJ/mol.
evidence: This is a result from the umbrella sampling MD simulations.

claim: The energy barrier for Kap95 to move across the Nsp1-lined pore is 6 kJ/mol.
source: The data show that the energy barrier that tCherry needs to overcome to move across the Nsp1-lined pore is approximately 12 kJ/mol, while for Kap95, it is much lower, 6 kJ/mol.
evidence: This is a result from the umbrella sampling MD simulations.

claim: For the Nsp1-S pore, the energy barriers are very similar for Kap95 and tCherry, viz., 6.5 kJ/mol and 6.4 kJ/mol, respectively.
source: For the Nsp1-S pore however, the barriers are very similar for Kap95 and tCherry, viz., 6.5 kJ/mol and 6.4 kJ/mol, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the umbrella sampling MD simulations.

claim: The high energy barrier for tCherry in Nsp1 pores is entirely due to the strong steric hindrance from the high-density Nsp1 pore (100 mg/ml density).
source: If we focus on the wild-type Nsp1 pores, we see that the energy barrier for tCherry is high, 12 kJ mol−1, i.e. almost 5 kBT. This is entirely due to the strong steric hindrance that the inert tCherry particle experiences when it aims to pass through the high-density Nsp1 pore (100 mg/ml density, see Figures 2C and 3A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PMF results based on the density distributions.

claim: Kap95 is strongly attracted by the hydrophobic and weakly positively-charged Nsp1 meshwork, resulting in an energy well around |z| = 30 nm.
source: In contrast, the PMF curve for Kap95 in the wild-type pore shows a drastically different behavior. Due to the hydrophobic binding sites and negative charge, the Kap95 particle is strongly attracted by the hydrophobic and weakly positively-charged Nsp1 meshwork, resulting in an energy well around |z| = 30 nm, which co-localizes with the high concentration of Nsp1 hydrophobic head groups (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PMF results based on the molecular interactions.

claim: The energy well for Kap95 co-localizes with the high concentration of Nsp1 hydrophobic head groups.
source: In contrast, the PMF curve for Kap95 in the wild-type pore shows a drastically different behavior. Due to the hydrophobic binding sites and negative charge, the Kap95 particle is strongly attracted by the hydrophobic and weakly positively-charged Nsp1 meshwork, resulting in an energy well around |z| = 30 nm, which co-localizes with the high concentration of Nsp1 hydrophobic head groups (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the PMF with the density distribution.

claim: From an energetic point of view, the Nsp1-S pore is non-selective for tCherry and Kap95.
source: Despite the fact that their specific energy profiles are different, the energy barriers calculated from the PMF curves are similar, 6.5 kJ mol−1 and 6.4 kJ mol−1 for tCherry and Kap95, respectively. Clearly, from an energetic point of view, the Nsp1-S pore thus is non-selective for the two particles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PMF calculations.

claim: Kap95 translocates through the nanopore coated with Nsp1 at a computed rate of 1.5 ± 0.3 Hz.
source: The computed event rates are compared to the experimental event rates in Figure 5B, showing excellent agreement (for details see Figure 5—figure supplement 3): Kap95 translocates through the nanopore coated with Nsp1 at a rate of 1.5 ± 0.3 Hz, while tCherry features a much lower rate of 0.13 ± 0.03 Hz.
evidence: This is a computed event rate using the Arrhenius relation.

claim: tCherry translocates through the nanopore coated with Nsp1 at a computed rate of 0.13 ± 0.03 Hz.
source: The computed event rates are compared to the experimental event rates in Figure 5B, showing excellent agreement (for details see Figure 5—figure supplement 3): Kap95 translocates through the nanopore coated with Nsp1 at a rate of 1.5 ± 0.3 Hz, while tCherry features a much lower rate of 0.13 ± 0.03 Hz.
evidence: This is a computed event rate using the Arrhenius relation.

claim: For the mutated pore, the computed frequencies are very similar: 1.3 ± 0.3 Hz for Kap95 and 1.2 ± 0.1 Hz for tCherry.

evidence: This is a computed event rate using the Arrhenius relation.

claim: The permeability barrier of Nsp1-S is compromised, while Nsp1 allows Kap95 but not tCherry, featuring a clear transport selectivity.
source: These results show that the permeability barrier of Nsp1-S is compromised, while Nsp1 allows Kap95 but not tCherry, featuring a clear transport selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and computational results.

claim: Nsp1 pores block the conductance stronger than Nsp1-S mutant pores.
source: Our results provide the first experimental data for the ion conductance as a function of nanopore diameter (5 to 65 nm) for Nsp1 pores. Nsp1 pores are found to block the conductance stronger than Nsp1-S mutant pores.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental conductance findings.

claim: For small pore sizes the conductance is low (<4 nS), similar but slightly larger than natural NPCs (~1 nS).
source: For small pore sizes the conductance is low (<4 nS), similar but slightly larger than natural NPCs (~1 nS) (Bustamante et al., 1995; Tonini et al., 1999).
evidence: This compares the experimental results to natural NPCs, with citations.

claim: The density in the Nsp1 pores exhibits a maximum at the pore center and remains significantly high throughout, even for pore radii much larger than two times the Stokes radius of Nsp1.
source: Interestingly, the density in the Nsp1 pores exhibits a maximum at the pore center and remains significantly high throughout (see Figure 2C and Figure 3A), even for pore radii that are much larger than two times the Stokes radius of Nsp1 (2RS ~ 15 nm).
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations shown in Figures 2C and 3A.

claim: The high density throughout Nsp1 pores can be partly attributed to the cohesive, sticky nature of the low-charge N-terminal 'head' segments rich in hydrophobic FG-repeats and partly to the geometric confinement of the closely-spaced Nups.
source: This can be partly attributed to the cohesive, sticky nature of the low-charge N-terminal 'head' segments of Nsp1 that are rich in hydrophobic FG-repeats and partly to the geometric confinement of the closely-spaced Nups in the channel (the grafting distance of 5.7 nm is considerably smaller than twice the Stokes radius (2RS ~15 nm).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the density distribution based on molecular properties.

claim: The findings are consistent with the work of Zahn et al. who found Nsp1 brush heights of approximately 27 nm for similar grafting densities.
source: This is consistent with the work of Zahn et al. (Zahn et al., 2016) who found Nsp1 brush heights of approximately 27 nm for similar grafting densities and with the work of Vovk et al., who found that for surface-tethered FG domains the brush height increases with decreasing grafting distance (Vovk et al., 2016).
evidence: This compares the results to previous work, with citations.

claim: Vovk et al. found that for surface-tethered FG domains the brush height increases with decreasing grafting distance.
source: This is consistent with the work of Zahn et al. (Zahn et al., 2016) who found Nsp1 brush heights of approximately 27 nm for similar grafting densities and with the work of Vovk et al., who found that for surface-tethered FG domains the brush height increases with decreasing grafting distance (Vovk et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites previous work on FG domain behavior.

claim: Nup98 pores exhibit a high-density, donut-like structure that are fully open at the center already at pore diameters of ~25 nm.
source: The spatial structure of the FG and SG domains in the wildtype and mutant Nsp1 pores shows a striking difference with that of (non-glycosylated) Nup98 pores that exhibit a high-density, donut-like structure that are fully open at the center already at pore diameters of ~25 nm.
evidence: This is an observation from the MD simulations comparing different Nup types.

claim: The donut-like structure in Nup98 is due to the lower geometric confinement (grafting distance approximately equal to 2RS = 8.2 nm) and the much larger Nup98 cohesiveness.
source: This is due to the lower geometric confinement (the grafting distance was measured to be approximately equal to 2RS = 8.2 nm) and the much larger Nup98 cohesiveness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural differences based on molecular properties.

claim: The ratio of charged over hydrophobic residues is 0.2 for Nup98 versus 0.9 and 1.6 for Nsp1 and Nsp1-S, respectively.
source: The latter reflects the smaller ratio of charged over hydrophobic residues (0.2 for Nup98 versus 0.9 and 1.6 for Nsp1 and Nsp1-S, respectively), resulting in characteristic protein densities of 344, 74, and 52 mg/ml, respectively (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a calculated property from the amino acid sequences.

claim: The characteristic protein densities are 344, 74, and 52 mg/ml for Nup98, Nsp1, and Nsp1-S, respectively.
source: The latter reflects the smaller ratio of charged over hydrophobic residues (0.2 for Nup98 versus 0.9 and 1.6 for Nsp1 and Nsp1-S, respectively), resulting in characteristic protein densities of 344, 74, and 52 mg/ml, respectively (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the MD simulations.

claim: The density-based conductance relation successfully predicts the very low conductance at small pore sizes and the non-linear transition to an access-resistance-dominated conductance for larger pores.
source: By adopting a single critical protein concentration, the model successfully predicts the very low conductance at small pore sizes and the non-linear transition to an access-resistance-dominated conductance for larger pores.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's predictive capability.

claim: The conductance of the Nsp1-coated pores was found to be lower than those coated with Nsp1-S, which is a direct consequence of the sequence-dependent difference in spatial FG-domain distribution.
source: The conductance of the Nsp1-coated pores was found to be lower than those coated with Nsp1-S, which is a direct consequence of the sequence-dependent difference in spatial FG-domain distribution as discussed above.
evidence: This is a conclusion linking the conductance measurements to the density distributions.

claim: The experimental and computational conductance data for Nup98 nanopores are in excellent agreement.
source: We also used the density-based conductance relation (Equation 2) to predict the conductance of the Nup98 nanopores published before (Kowalczyk et al., 2011b) (see Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Also in this case the experimental and computational data are in excellent agreement, demonstrating the broad applicability of the G(d) relation for Nup-nanopores that feature profoundly different protein density distributions.
evidence: This is a validation of the model using previously published data, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The differences between the Nsp1 and Nsp1-S biomimetic pores testify to the importance of the hydrophobic residues for barrier-formation by FG domains.
source: The differences between the Nsp1 and Nsp1-S biomimetic pores testify to the importance of the hydrophobic residues for barrier-formation by FG domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative experimental results.

claim: The formation of hydrogels and surface-grafted FG domains showed evidence of the FG motifs' role in establishing the cohesiveness of Nsp1 relative to Nsp1-S.
source: The formation of hydrogels (Ribbeck and Görlich, 2001; Frey et al., 2006) and surface-grafted FG domains (Eisele et al., 2013) similarly showed evidence of the FG motifs' role in establishing the cohesiveness of Nsp1 relative to Nsp1-S.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hexanediols have been shown to disrupt the permeability barrier of either human or yeast NPCs.
source: Hexanediols have been shown to disrupt the permeability barrier of either human or yeast NPCs (Lim et al., 2007; Patel et al., 2007; Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The FG motifs not only establish a cohesive structure, they also assist transport of NTRs through the NPC channel.
source: Moreover, the FG motifs not only establish a cohesive structure (Frey et al., 2006; Patel et al., 2007; Yamada et al., 2010; Hülsmann et al., 2012), they also assist transport of NTRs through the NPC channel (Rout and Wente, 1994; Bayliss et al., 1999; Bayliss et al., 2002; Isgro and Schulten, 2005; Port et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The dwell time of Kap95 through Nsp1-coated pores (~5 ms) is close to the 3 to 10 ms NTR passage times observed through the NPC.
source: We observed that Kap95 translocates well through Nsp1-coated pores, with sizeable (few ms) dwell times, compared to the fast translocation through bare and Nsp1-S-coated pores. Note that the dwell time of ~5 ms is close to the 3 to 10 ms NTR passage times observed through the NPC (Yang et al., 2004; Kubitscheck et al., 2005), which is remarkable given the simplicity of our biomimetic NPCs.
evidence: This compares the experimental results to natural NPCs, with citations.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In a previous report, Nsp1-based artificial NPCs were tested for selective behavior of various NTRs and NTR-cargo complexes which translocated effortlessly whereas the mutant version of NTR (with reduced binding affinity to the FG repeats) transported at a much lower rate.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.
